newsitem.title: INDIA: India privatisation panel delays oil firms' sale.
newsitem.headline: India privatisation panel delays oil firms' sale.

text.p: India's Disinvestment Commission said on Friday it was deferring a decision on privatising two state-controlled oil firms until the government decided to free domestic petroleum prices.

Commission chairman G.V. Ramakrishna told a news conference that the panel had also recommended certain structural changes within Oil India Ltd (OIL) and the Oil and Natural Gas Corp (ONGC) before shares could be sold off.
"Until the (oil) pricing policy is clarified, we feel we will not get the best prices for these companies," Ramakrishna said.
"Even if the government makes an announcement that it plans to dismantle the administered pricing mechanism (APM), their share prices will be significantly higher," he said.

India controls the domestic prices of petroleum products, fixing some of them well below global prices. By the end of 1996/97 (April-March), the government owed state-controlled oil firms 155 billion rupees ($4.3 billion).
OIL, India's second-largest oil producer after ONGC, is 97 percent owned by the government, with its employees holding the remaining three percent.
"The current policy of APM denies a proper value for (OIL's) output," the commission said in a report presented to the government on Thursday.

It said privatising OIL "could be considered after a year or so when the company's own prospects would be clearly established through the outcome of exploration activities...and the government's policy on APM".

ONGC, which accounts for nearly 90 percent of India's oil and gas production, reported in April that net profit for 1996/97 (April-March) rose slightly to 19.75 billion rupees from 19.45 billion in the previous year.
On ONGC, the report said: "The switchover from APM to international prices for its production would add considerably to ONGC's operating margins and profits."
"The Commission recommends that disinvestment in ONGC be considered only after organisational changes are in position and the new pricing policy is known."

The government has been wavering for months over a decision on raising oil prices. Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral said on Thursday the mounting subsidy was unsustainable and an increase in petroleum prices was inevitable, but did not say when the price hike would occur.

"All said and done, this dithering on the part of the government and lack of resolute action is eroding the market perception about the value of these two companies," said R.K. Pachauri, director of the Tata Energy Research Institute.
"Disinvestment to bring about structural changes is one aspect," he told Reuters.

"The other is to ensure the government gets its due once disinvestment actually takes place. The government wouldn't like to lose money if there is a prospect of gaining some money through an action which will anyway take place," he said.
